module_title: Forging Your First Project: A Basic Hook

lessons.title: Selecting and Cutting Stock for a Hook
lessons.body: For your first hook, choose mild steel round bar, 10mm to 12mm diameter. This size is easy to heat and move by hand, yet strong enough for hanging pots, tools, or lanterns. In many African markets, you can buy offcuts from welding workshops or scrap yards. Look for clean, rust-free pieces. Avoid galvanized or painted metalâthe fumes are toxic when heated. A good length is 30cm to 40cm. That gives you enough to form the hook and a mounting plate or eye. If you only have a long bar, cut it with a hacksaw or a hot cut on the anvil. For a hot cut, heat the bar to bright orange (about 900Â°C), place it over the anvil's cutting edge, and strike with a chisel or the edge of your hammer. Remember to cut on the far side of the anvil so the cut piece doesn't fly. For a cold cut, clamp the bar in a vise and use a hacksaw with 18 to 24 teeth per inch. Add a few drops of oil to ease the cut. After cutting, smooth the ends with a file or grinder. If you don't have a vise, lay the bar on a wooden block and secure it with your foot. Always wear safety glasses and gloves. In rural areas, a machete or axe can score the metal, but a hacksaw is safer and more precise. Once cut, you're ready to forge.

lessons.title: Drawing Out the Hook Point
lessons.body: Drawing out means stretching the metal to make it longer and thinner. Heat one end of your 10mm bar to a bright yellow-orange (about 1000Â°C). Hold it on the anvil with tongs. Strike the hot end with the flat face of your hammer, aiming slightly downward to taper the tip. Work from the tip back toward the middle. Use a series of overlapping blowsâabout 20 to 30 strikesâturning the bar 90 degrees every few hits to keep it square or round. If the metal cools below cherry red (around 700Â°C), stop and reheat. Forging cold causes cracks. You want a point that is about 5mm thick at the tip and tapers over 8cm to 10cm. This point will become the sharp end of the hook. To make a neat taper, use the horn of the anvil for curves or the flat face for straight tapers. If you have a cross-peen hammer, use the peen to stretch faster, then smooth with the flat face. Check your work oftenâhold it up to the light to see if the taper is even. In many African smithies, a simple charcoal forge with a hand-cranked blower works well. Keep your fire clean and focused. After drawing out, you may need to straighten the bar by tapping it on the anvil. Don't rush; a good point makes the hook look professional.

lessons.title: Forming the Hook Curve
lessons.body: Now you'll bend the pointed end into a J-shaped curve. Heat the middle section of the barâabout 10cm from the pointâto a bright orange. Place the hot section over the horn of the anvil. The horn's rounded shape helps you form a smooth curve. Using your hammer, strike the bar gently, bending it around the horn. Work from the point backward, making a curve that is about 5cm in diameter. Don't hit too hard; you want a controlled bend, not a kink. If you don't have a horn, use a pipe or a thick metal rod clamped in a vise. For a tighter hook, bend around a smaller diameter. For a larger hook, use a bigger form. Once the basic curve is formed, check it by eye. The curve should be even and the point should face inward, parallel to the shank. If it's uneven, reheat and adjust. You can also use a bending forkâa tool that fits in the hardy holeâto fine-tune the curve. Remember to keep the metal hot; bending cold can cause cracks. After bending, you may want to flatten the curve slightly with a hammer to give it a forged look. This also strengthens the hook. In Africa, hooks are used for hanging pots over fires, so make sure the curve is deep enough to hold a handle securely. Test it with a stick or a pot handle. A good hook curve is the heart of your project.

lessons.title: Twisting the Hook for Decoration
lessons.body: A decorative twist adds beauty and shows off your skill. Heat the straight section of the barâbetween the hook curve and the opposite endâto a bright orange. You'll need a vise and a wrench or twisting bar. Clamp one end of the heated section in the vise. Grip the other end with a wrench or a pair of tongs with a twisting bar. Turn the wrench clockwise or counterclockwise to create a spiral. For a uniform twist, apply steady pressure and turn the same number of times. A good twist for a 10mm bar is about 3 to 4 full turns over 5cm. If you turn too much, the metal may crack. If you don't have a vise, you can twist by holding one end with tongs and the other with a hammer handle through the eyeâbut a vise is safer. After twisting, you may want to flatten the twist slightly with a hammer to create a faceted look. This also makes the twist more pronounced. Reheat as needed. Twisting is best done when the metal is at a consistent orange heat. If it cools, stop and reheat. Once twisted, straighten the bar if it bent during twisting. A decorative twist not only looks good but also adds strength. In many African cultures, twisted ironwork is traditional and adds value to your product. Practice on a scrap piece first to get the feel. Then apply the twist to your hook.

lessons.title: Finishing the Hook: Brushing and Waxing
lessons.body: Finishing makes your hook look professional and protects it from rust. Start by letting the hook cool to room temperature. Use a wire brushâhand brush or wire wheel on a drillâto remove scale and smooth the surface. Brush in one direction to create a nice grain. If you have a bench grinder with a wire wheel, that's faster. For a shiny finish, sand with 80-grit then 120-grit emery cloth. Next, heat the hook again to about 200Â°Câjust hot enough that a drop of water sizzles. You can do this in your forge or with a torch. Then apply a thin coat of beeswax or paraffin wax using a cloth or a brush. The heat melts the wax, which soaks into the metal and creates a protective black finish. Rub the wax in while the hook is hot. Let it cool, then buff with a clean cloth. For a darker finish, you can use linseed oil instead of wax. Heat the hook to about 300Â°C and apply oil with a rag; it will smoke and polymerize, leaving a tough coating. Repeat two or three times. In Africa, beeswax is often available from local beekeepers. Avoid using motor oilâit's toxic. After waxing, your hook should have a smooth, slightly glossy finish. Check for any sharp edges and file them smooth. A well-finished hook can be sold or used immediately. Hang it by the eye or mounting plate.

lessons.title: Evaluating Your Work and Identifying Flaws
lessons.body: After finishing, inspect your hook critically. Look for common flaws: cracks, uneven curves, cold shuts (folds where metal didn't weld), and hammer marks. Cracks often occur if you forged too cold or overheated the steel. If you see a crack, it's best to start overâcracks weaken the hook. Uneven curves can be fixed by reheating and bending, but if the hook is already waxed, you'll need to remove the finish first. Cold shuts happen when you strike with a hammer that has a sharp edge or when you fold metal without welding. They look like lines or overlaps. If a cold shut is deep, discard the hook. Hammer marks are normal but should be smooth. You can file them out. Check the twist: it should be even and not too tight. Check the point: it should be centered and sharp, not off to one side. Test the hook by hanging a weightâstart with 5kg, then 10kg. A good hook should hold at least 20kg without bending. If it bends, the metal may be too soft or the curve too shallow. Also check the eye or mounting holeâit should be smooth and not cut into the metal. Finally, compare your hook to a professional example. Ask yourself: Would I buy this? If not, note what to improve next time. Keep a log of your mistakes and successes. Practice makes perfect.

lessons.title: Practical Reference
lessons.body:
Practical Reference: Forging Your First Project â A Basic Hook

This practical reference supports the RISE AFRICA Skills module Forging Your First Project: A Basic Hook. It is written for the working smith, the farm workshop, the vocational trainee, and the small enterprise that sells finished ironwork at local markets, hardware stores, or to construction clients. A basic hook is a low-cost, high-demand product. In much of Africa it is used for hanging tools, securing gates, lifting sacks, drying fish, and supporting tarpaulins. Mastery of the hook is therefore not only a training exercise; it is a route to cash flow. This reference gives you the measurements, stock choices, forming steps, finishing methods, and quality checks you need to produce hooks consistently and sell them profitably.

1. Selecting and Cutting Stock for a Hook

The hook is normally forged from mild steel round bar. For a general-purpose utility hook, 8 mm to 12 mm diameter is the most practical range. Smaller stock (6 mm) is suitable for light domestic hooks; larger stock (16 mm and above) is used for heavy lifting or structural hooks where the load may exceed 100 kg. In many African markets, stock is sold by length, by weight, or by the piece, and availability varies between urban steel merchants and rural scrap yards. Where new stock is unavailable, vehicle leaf springs, reinforcing bar offcuts, and old gate rods can be recycled, but these must be inspected for cracks and excessive corrosion before use.

Cutting should be done with a hacksaw for small diameters, a bolt cutter for up to 12 mm, or a hot cut with a cold chisel on the anvil for larger stock. Always allow an extra 15â20 mm on the cut length for the point and the finishing allowance. A common beginner error is cutting too short, which leaves no material for drawing out the point or forming the eye.

2. Drawing Out the Hook Point

Drawing out is the process of reducing the cross-section of the steel while increasing its length. For the hook point, heat the last 40â50 mm of the stock to a bright orange (approximately 900â1000Â°C) and hammer it on the horn or the edge of the anvil. Rotate the stock a quarter turn between blows so the taper remains square and symmetrical. The point should taper from the full stock diameter to about 3â4 mm over a length of 40â60 mm. Do not overheat the steel; if it sparks excessively, it is burning and will become brittle.

In a rural African workshop, charcoal or coal is the common fuel. Forge welding and drawing out require a clean, reducing fire. A simple side-blast forge made from a car brake drum and a hand-cranked blower is adequate. Keep the fire slightly green (excess fuel) to avoid oxidation. A useful rule for small enterprises: one person can draw out a hook point in 2â3 heats, which means a production rate of 15â25 hooks per day depending on stock size and skill.

3. Forming the Hook Curve

The curve is formed over the horn of the anvil or a bending fork. Heat the middle of the drawn section to a uniform orange and bend it progressively, not in one heavy blow. For a standard utility hook, the opening (the gap between the point and the shank) should be 40â60 mm, and the bend radius should be smooth, without flats or kinks. A common mistake is bending cold, which causes cracking, especially in recycled steel. If the steel is high-carbon or of unknown origin, normalize it after bending by heating to a dull red and allowing it to cool slowly in air or ash.

4. Twisting the Hook for Decoration

Decorative twisting adds market value without adding much material cost. Heat a 60â80 mm section of the shank to a uniform orange, clamp one end in a vice or hold it with tongs, and apply a steady twisting force with a wrench or a second pair of tongs. Count the turns; 2â4 full twists are usually enough for a decorative hook. Twisting too cold will crack the steel. Twisting too hot will produce a rough, scaly surface. After twisting, straighten the shank and reheat for the next operation. In tourist markets from Nairobi to Accra, twisted hooks can sell for 20â40% more than plain hooks because they are perceived as handcrafted.

5. Finishing the Hook: Brushing and Waxing

Finishing determines whether the hook looks professional and resists rust. First, brush the hot hook with a wire brush while it is still at a black heat (about 400â500Â°C). This removes scale and produces a smooth, dark surface. Then apply a thin coat of beeswax, paraffin wax, or a mixture of wax and linseed oil. The wax melts into the warm steel and forms a protective film. For outdoor hooks, a second coat of linseed oil or a locally available anti-rust paint is recommended. In humid coastal regions, zinc-rich paint or galvanizing is preferable, but waxing is the cheapest and most accessible method for small workshops.

â  SAFETY WARNING â HOT METAL AND FUMES

Always wear leather gloves, safety glasses, and a leather apron when forging. Never quench hot steel in water without eye protection; steam and spitting water can cause severe burns. Waxing produces smoke and fumes â work outdoors or in a well-ventilated area. Keep a bucket of sand, not water, near the forge for fire emergencies. In many African workshops, open fires and hand-cranked blowers are used; ensure the forge is on a non-combustible surface and that children and visitors are kept at a safe distance. Burns are the most common injury in blacksmithing, and most are preventable with basic PPE and discipline.

6. Evaluating Your Work and Identifying Flaws

Quality control protects your reputation and your income. Check every hook for the following defects:

Flaw Cause Effect Correction
Crack at the bend Bending cold or overheating Hook may snap under load Reheat, normalize, re-bend; discard if crack is deep
Off-centre point Uneven hammer blows Poor appearance, weak tip Reheat and re-draw with quarter turns
Scale pits Oxidizing fire or too much air blast Rough surface, rust traps Use a reducing fire; brush hot
Uneven twist Inconsistent heat or force Weak decorative value Reheat, re-twist with steady pressure
Sharp edges on eye Poor finishing Cuts rope or hand File or grind smooth before waxing

Source: Adapted from Blacksmithing: A Manual for Rural Schools (FAO/UNESCO, 1986) and field observations from RISE AFRICA vocational workshops in East and West Africa.

7. Business Notes for African Smiths

A basic hook is a fast-moving product. In many markets, a 150 mm hook made from 10 mm mild steel sells for the equivalent of US$1.50â4.00, depending on finish and location. The material cost is often less than US$0.50 if stock is bought in bulk or recycled. Labour time is 15â25 minutes for a trained smith. That means a single smith working a six-hour day can produce 15â20 hooks and generate a gross margin of US$15â60 per day, before fuel and overheads. The key business levers are:

  • Standardise sizes: Offer three sizes (small, medium, heavy) so customers can order repeatably.
  • Bundle for resale: Sell packs of 5 or 10 to hardware shops and construction sites.
  • Add value: Twisted or painted hooks command higher prices.
  • Reduce fuel cost: Use a covered forge, dry fuel, and batch production to keep the fire hot.
  • Record costs: Track steel, fuel, and time per hook to know your true profit.

8. Stock and Production Data

Hook Type Stock Diameter Typical Length Load Guide Typical Market Use
Light domestic 6 mm 100â130 mm Up to 10 kg Kitchen, hanging clothes, small tools
General utility 8â10 mm 150â200 mm 10â40 kg Farm tools, sacks, tarpaulins
Heavy duty 12â16 mm 200â300 mm 40â120 kg Gate hardware, lifting, construction
Decorative / tourist 6â10 mm 120â180 mm Up to 20 kg Craft markets, gifts, interior fittings

Source: Load guides are indicative and based on mild steel safety factors; actual capacity depends on steel grade, heat treatment, and installation. Reference: FAO/UNESCO Blacksmithing Manual, 1986, and Practical Action Technical Brief: Blacksmithing.

Quick Reference Checklist

  1. Select mild steel round bar: 6â16 mm depending on load; inspect for cracks and rust.
  2. Cut stock with 15â20 mm allowance for point and finishing.
  3. Heat to bright orange (900â1000Â°C) before drawing out; never forge cold.
  4. Draw the point symmetrically with quarter turns; taper to 3â4 mm.
  5. Form the curve over the horn; keep the opening 40â60 mm for utility hooks.
  6. Twist only when hot; 2â4 turns for decoration; re-straighten the shank.
  7. Brush hot at black heat, then wax or oil immediately for rust protection.
  8. Inspect for cracks, off-centre points, scale pits, and sharp edges before selling.

Further Reading

  • FAO â Blacksmithing: A Manual for Rural Schools (free, official FAO publication).
  • Practical Action â Knowledge Centre: Blacksmithing and Metalwork Technical Briefs (free registration may be required).
  • ILO â Vocational Training and Skills Development Resources (free official guides).
  • UNIDO â Small Enterprise and Metalworking Resources (free publications and toolkits).
  • African Development Bank â SME and Skills Development Documents (free official reports).

Prepared for RISE AFRICA Skills â Basic Blacksmithing. This practical reference is intended for training and enterprise development. Always follow local safety regulations and use appropriate personal protective equipment.

quiz.q: What is the recommended diameter for mild steel round bar for a first hook?
quiz.explanation: 10mm to 12mm is easy to forge by hand and strong enough for most hooks.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid galvanized metal in the forge?
options: B) It melts at low temperatures
C) It releases toxic fumes when heated
D) It is too hard to cut
quiz.explanation: Galvanized coatings contain zinc, which gives off poisonous fumes when heated.

quiz.q: What is the ideal length of stock for a basic hook?
quiz.explanation: 30cm to 40cm provides enough material for the hook and mounting end.

quiz.q: When hot cutting, what color should the metal be?
quiz.explanation: Bright orange (about 900Â°C) is the right temperature for hot cutting.

quiz.q: What is the purpose of drawing out the hook point?
options: B) To taper and lengthen the end
C) To bend it into a curve
quiz.explanation: Drawing out stretches the metal to create a tapered point.

quiz.q: What forging temperature range is best for drawing out?
quiz.explanation: Mild steel forges well between 800Â°C and 1000Â°C (cherry red to yellow-orange).

quiz.q: Why should you turn the bar 90 degrees while drawing out?
options: A) To keep the taper even
quiz.explanation: Turning prevents the bar from becoming lopsided and keeps the taper symmetrical.

quiz.q: What happens if you forge metal below cherry red?
quiz.explanation: Forging too cold causes stress and cracks in the metal.

quiz.q: Which part of the anvil is best for forming a hook curve?
quiz.explanation: The horn's rounded shape helps create smooth curves.

quiz.q: What is the recommended diameter of the hook curve?
quiz.explanation: A 5cm curve is a good size for hanging pots and tools.

quiz.q: What tool can be used instead of an anvil horn for bending?
options: B) A pipe or metal rod
quiz.explanation: A pipe or rod clamped in a vise can serve as a bending form.

quiz.q: Why should you keep the metal hot while bending?
quiz.explanation: Cold bending can cause cracks; hot bending is safer and easier.

quiz.q: What is a bending fork used for?
quiz.explanation: A bending fork fits in the hardy hole and helps adjust curves.

quiz.q: After bending, why might you flatten the curve slightly?
options: B) To give a forged look and add strength
quiz.explanation: Flattening adds a hand-forged texture and can strengthen the hook.

quiz.q: What is the ideal temperature for twisting?
quiz.explanation: Bright orange (about 1000Â°C) is ideal for twisting without cracking.

quiz.q: How many full turns are recommended for a decorative twist on a 10mm bar?
quiz.explanation: 3 to 4 turns over 5cm gives a nice twist without over-stressing the metal.

quiz.q: What tool is essential for holding one end during twisting?
quiz.explanation: A vise securely holds the metal while you twist the other end.

quiz.q: Why might you flatten a twist after making it?
options: A) To make it less visible
B) To create a faceted look and add strength
quiz.explanation: Flattening the twist gives a decorative faceted appearance and strengthens it.

quiz.q: What should you do if the metal cools during twisting?
quiz.explanation: Twisting cold metal can cause cracks; reheat to bright orange.

quiz.q: What is the first step in finishing a hook?
quiz.explanation: Wire brushing removes scale and smooths the surface before further finishing.

quiz.q: What temperature should the hook be for waxing?
quiz.explanation: About 200Â°C is hot enough for wax to melt and penetrate without burning.

quiz.q: Which wax is recommended for finishing?
quiz.explanation: Beeswax or paraffin wax provides a protective finish; motor oil is toxic.

quiz.q: What is an alternative to wax for a dark finish?
quiz.explanation: Linseed oil heated on metal polymerizes to a tough, dark coating.

quiz.q: Why should you avoid motor oil for finishing?
options: D) It makes the metal brittle
quiz.explanation: Motor oil contains harmful chemicals and should not be heated on metal.

quiz.q: What is a cold shut?
options: B) A fold or lap in the metal
quiz.explanation: A cold shut is a flaw where metal folds over without welding, creating a weak spot.

quiz.q: What might cause cracks in a forged hook?
quiz.explanation: Forging below cherry red can cause stress cracks.

quiz.q: How can you test the strength of your hook?
options: A) Hit it with a hammer
C) Drop it on the floor
quiz.explanation: Hanging increasing weights (e.g., 5kg, 10kg, 20kg) tests load capacity.

quiz.q: What is a sign of a well-formed hook point?
options: B) It is sharp and centered
quiz.explanation: A good point is centered, tapered, and sharp for easy use.

quiz.q: Why should you keep a log of your work?
options: B) To track mistakes and improvements
quiz.explanation: A log helps you learn from errors and improve your skills.

quiz.q: What should you do if you find a deep cold shut in your hook?
quiz.explanation: A deep cold shut weakens the hook and cannot be reliably fixed.
